subject: biology

items.q: A motor neuron has its cell body in the spinal cord and a single fibre about 1 m long that reaches a muscle in the foot. What is this fibre?
items.correct: An axon: a single long fibre along which impulses are conducted away from the cell body.
items.misconception: One of the neuron's several axons, each of which reaches a different muscle in the leg.
items.why: Diagrams show the axon branching into many terminals near its end, and multipolar neurons show many fibres leaving the cell body, so students count each branch or each fibre as an axon. An axon is a long single fibre. Dendrites are multiple shorter fibres. The branches at the end of an axon are terminals of the same single axon, not separate axons.
items.specStatementText: A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
items.random_wrong: A nerve, because a fibre this long must be made of many neurons joined end to end.

items.q: How does the sodium–potassium pump contribute to the resting potential of a neuron?
items.correct: It uses energy from ATP to move sodium ions out of the neuron and potassium ions in, building up concentration gradients of both ions.
items.misconception: It uses energy from ATP to move potassium ions out of the neuron and sodium ions in across the membrane, building up concentration gradients of both ions.
items.why: Sodium is named first in 'sodium–potassium pump' and sodium is the ion that rushes in during an action potential, so students remember sodium as the 'inside' ion. The sodium–potassium pump moves sodium ions out of the neuron and potassium ions into it. The resulting gradients mean sodium ions are more concentrated outside and potassium ions inside; it is these gradients that allow sodium ions to enter during an action potential.
items.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
items.random_wrong: It lets sodium and potassium ions diffuse down their concentration gradients through its channel, without using any ATP at all.

items.q: Measurements on a resting neuron show that potassium ions are about 30 times more concentrated inside than outside and sodium ions about 10 times more concentrated outside than inside, yet the inside is at −70 mV relative to the outside. Which explanation of the negative resting potential is consistent with these measurements?
items.correct: The pump moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in, and potassium ions leak back out faster than sodium ions leak in.
items.misconception: All the positively charged ions are pumped out of the cytoplasm by the sodium–potassium pump, leaving only negatively charged ions inside the neuron.
items.why: The 'inside negative' label on diagrams is read as meaning the cytoplasm contains only negative charge, and the high potassium ion concentration inside is forgotten. The cytoplasm contains many positive ions, especially potassium ions. The resting potential is negative because slightly more positive charge leaves than enters (three sodium ions out per two potassium ions in, and greater leakage of potassium ions outwards) and because negatively charged proteins are held inside.
items.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
items.random_wrong: Positive ions diffuse out through the pump faster than they diffuse in, because the pump is simply a channel that favours movement outwards.

items.q: A neuron is treated with a chemical that stops it producing ATP. Which prediction about its resting potential is correct?
items.correct: It gradually falls towards zero, because the pump stops and the ion gradients run down as ions leak across the membrane.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because a neuron at rest is inactive and does not need to use ATP for anything until an impulse arrives.
items.why: The word 'resting' suggests nothing is happening, and the resting potential is drawn as a flat line on a trace. The resting potential is generated and maintained by pumping, which requires energy from ATP. If ATP supply stops, the gradients gradually run down and the resting potential is lost.
items.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, because the pump moves ions passively down their gradients and does not need ATP in order to work.

items.q: Why is a nerve impulse described as an electrical signal?
items.correct: It consists of positively charged ions moving across the membrane, which changes the membrane potential.
items.misconception: It consists of electrons flowing along the inside of the fibre, in the same way as a current in a metal wire.
items.why: Nerve impulses are described as 'electrical' and the nervous system is compared to wiring, so the only electrical current students know, electron flow in a wire, is transferred to the axon. A nerve impulse is electrical because it involves movement of positively charged ions (sodium and potassium ions) across the membrane, not the movement of electrons along the fibre.
items.specStatementText: A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
items.random_wrong: It consists of neurotransmitter molecules travelling along the fibre and carrying their electrical charge with them.

items.q: Electrodes inside and outside an axon show that the inside briefly becomes positive relative to the outside as an impulse passes. What causes this change?
items.correct: Sodium ions move into the axon across the membrane at that point.
items.misconception: Potassium ions move into the axon across the membrane at that point.
items.why: The two ions are learned as a pair that move in opposite directions, and the direction of each is easily swapped, especially because the pump moves them the other way from the channels. During an action potential sodium ions diffuse into the axon, making the inside positive (depolarization). Potassium ions then diffuse out, making the inside negative again (repolarization). The pump later moves sodium ions out and potassium ions in to restore the gradients.
items.specStatementText: A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
items.random_wrong: Electrons move out of the axon along the inner surface of its membrane.

items.q: Conduction speeds were measured in three nerve fibres. Fibre P (a squid giant axon) is non-myelinated, 500 µm in diameter, and conducts at 25 m s⁻¹. Fibre Q is non-myelinated, 1 µm in diameter, and conducts at 1 m s⁻¹. Fibre R is myelinated, 10 µm in diameter, and conducts at 60 m s⁻¹. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: Speed rises with diameter in non-myelinated fibres, and myelination lets a narrow fibre conduct faster than a much wider one.
items.misconception: Myelin speeds up fibre R because the myelin sheath itself conducts the electrical current along the length of the fibre.
items.why: Myelin is described as 'speeding up' the impulse, and in the wiring analogy the thing that carries current quickly is a good conductor, so students give myelin the role of a conductor rather than an insulator. Myelin insulates the fibre. Ion channels and pumps are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier, and the action potential is propagated from node to node, which is faster than depolarizing the whole membrane.
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.random_wrong: Diameter has no effect on speed, so the difference between P and Q must be caused by the type of animal they came from.

items.q: In a study of axon diameter and conduction speed, the correlation coefficient was r = +0.90. Which statement about the coefficient of determination is correct?
items.correct: R² = 0.81, so about 81% of the variation in speed is explained by variation in diameter.
items.misconception: R² = 0.90, so about 90% of the variation in speed is explained by the variation in diameter.
items.why: Both r and R² are reported as decimals between 0 and 1, and the extra step of squaring is easily forgotten or thought not to matter. The coefficient of determination R² is the square of the correlation coefficient. It, not r, gives the degree to which variation in the independent variable explains variation in the dependent variable.
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.random_wrong: R² = 0.81, so about 81% of the fibres measured conducted faster when they had a larger diameter.

items.q: Across a range of animal species, the correlation coefficient between body size and nerve impulse conduction speed was r = −0.85. What does this value show?
items.correct: A strong negative correlation: speed tends to fall as body size rises, and R² is about 0.72.
items.misconception: A weak correlation, because a negative coefficient shows a smaller effect than a positive one would.
items.why: In everyday language 'negative' means bad or lacking, and students transfer this to the coefficient instead of reading the sign as the direction of the slope. The correlation coefficient runs from −1 to +1. Values close to −1 or +1 both indicate strong correlations; the sign only shows whether the variables rise together (positive) or one falls as the other rises (negative).
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.random_wrong: That an increase in body size is the direct cause of slower impulses in the larger species.

items.q: Which statement about a synapse is correct?
items.correct: A signal can pass across it in one direction only, from the presynaptic cell to the postsynaptic cell.
items.misconception: A signal can pass across it in either direction, depending on which of the two neurons is stimulated first.
items.why: Students picture the synapse as a simple gap or a wire junction, which would let a signal pass either way, and do not consider that the two sides have different structures. Only the presynaptic neuron has vesicles of neurotransmitter and only the postsynaptic membrane has receptors, so a signal can pass in one direction only across a typical synapse.
items.specStatementText: Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
items.random_wrong: It is found only where two neurons meet, so muscle fibres are stimulated directly by the nerve impulse.

items.q: Why can a signal pass in only one direction across a synapse?
items.correct: Only the presynaptic neuron stores neurotransmitter in vesicles, and only the postsynaptic membrane has receptors for it.
items.misconception: Electric current can only cross the cleft from the more positive presynaptic membrane to the more negative postsynaptic one.
items.why: The impulse is electrical and the cleft is drawn as a tiny gap, so students assume the electricity simply bridges it, like a spark across a spark plug. At a synapse the arriving action potential causes release of neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Transmission across the cleft is chemical, not electrical.
items.specStatementText: Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
items.random_wrong: Calcium ions can only diffuse across the cleft from the presynaptic side, because that is where they are concentrated.

items.q: What is the role of calcium ions in the release of neurotransmitter from a presynaptic neuron?
items.correct: Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane opens calcium channels; calcium ions enter and signal vesicles to fuse with the membrane.
items.misconception: Calcium ions are released from the presynaptic neuron and diffuse across the cleft, where they then depolarize the postsynaptic membrane.
items.why: Calcium is the first substance to move when the impulse arrives, so students give it the role of messenger and confuse it with the neurotransmitter. Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane causes uptake of calcium ions into the presynaptic neuron, where they act as a signalling chemical that causes vesicles to release neurotransmitter. It is the neurotransmitter that crosses the cleft.
items.specStatementText: Calcium entry triggers neurotransmitter release
items.random_wrong: Calcium ions have no role, because neurotransmitter simply diffuses out through the presynaptic membrane when an impulse arrives.

items.q: Calcium ions were removed from the fluid around a synapse. When the presynaptic neuron was stimulated, action potentials still reached the presynaptic terminal, but no response was recorded in the postsynaptic neuron. What does this result show?
items.correct: Entry of calcium ions is needed for neurotransmitter to be released, but not for the impulse to reach the terminal.
items.misconception: The neurotransmitter should have diffused out regardless, so the postsynaptic receptors must have been damaged.
items.why: Diffusion is the default mechanism students reach for, and the vesicles in synapse diagrams are treated as storage only, not as the means of release. Neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles. Calcium ions entering the presynaptic neuron signal the vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing the neurotransmitter into the cleft by exocytosis.
items.specStatementText: Calcium entry triggers neurotransmitter release
items.random_wrong: Calcium ions are the chemical that normally crosses the cleft and stimulates the postsynaptic neuron to respond.

items.q: How does acetylcholine generate an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
items.correct: It diffuses across the cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors, opening channels through which sodium ions enter the postsynaptic cell.
items.misconception: It diffuses across the cleft and enters the postsynaptic cell, where it depolarizes the membrane from the inside.
items.why: Diagrams show neurotransmitter moving from one cell towards the other, and the signal clearly ends up 'in' the next neuron, so the molecule is assumed to go in too. Neurotransmitter binds to transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Binding opens channels through which positively charged ions enter, generating an excitatory postsynaptic potential; the neurotransmitter remains in the cleft until it is broken down or taken up.
items.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
items.random_wrong: It is actively transported across the cleft by carrier proteins, which use ATP to push it into the postsynaptic cell.

items.q: A motor neuron forms a neuromuscular junction with a skeletal muscle fibre. Which statement about acetylcholine at this junction is correct?
items.correct: It is the same neurotransmitter used at many synapses between neurons, and here it binds to receptors on the muscle fibre membrane.
items.misconception: It is found only at neuromuscular junctions, because synapses between two neurons use different neurotransmitters.
items.why: Acetylcholine is usually introduced through the neuromuscular junction, and students assume neurotransmitters are specific to a location in the way that hormones are specific to target organs. Acetylcholine is used at many types of synapse, including synapses between neurons in the brain and nervous system as well as neuromuscular junctions.
items.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
items.random_wrong: It cannot be involved here, because synapses form only between two neurons and the muscle fibre is stimulated electrically.

items.q: Which sequence of events produces depolarization and then repolarization during an action potential?
items.correct: Voltage-gated sodium channels open at threshold and sodium ions enter; these channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave.
items.misconception: Voltage-gated sodium channels open at threshold and sodium ions enter; the sodium–potassium pump then actively pumps the sodium ions back out to repolarize the membrane.
items.why: The pump is the mechanism students learn for the resting potential, so they assume it must also be the mechanism for returning to that potential after an action potential. Repolarization is caused by potassium ions leaving through voltage-gated potassium channels, which is fast. The pump works continuously and only restores the small changes in concentration gradient afterwards; it is far too slow to repolarize the membrane in a millisecond.
items.specStatementText: Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
items.random_wrong: Voltage-gated potassium channels open at threshold and potassium ions enter; these then close and voltage-gated sodium channels open, so sodium ions leave.

items.q: The resting potential of a neuron is −70 mV and its threshold potential is −55 mV. A weak stimulus depolarizes the membrane to −60 mV. What happens next?
items.correct: The membrane returns to rest: threshold was not reached, so voltage-gated sodium channels stay closed.
items.misconception: A small action potential is produced, in proportion to the size of the stimulus that was applied to the membrane.
items.why: In most everyday systems a bigger input gives a bigger output, and the threshold is easily forgotten once the sequence of channel events has been memorized. A threshold potential must be reached for voltage-gated sodium channels to open. Once it is reached the channels open fully, so the action potential is all-or-nothing; below threshold no action potential occurs.
items.specStatementText: Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
items.random_wrong: The membrane has become hyperpolarized, so no action potential can be produced until it recovers to −70 mV.

items.q: A drug blocks the voltage-gated potassium channels in an axon. Which effect on its action potentials is predicted?
items.correct: Depolarization occurs normally, but repolarization is much slower, so each action potential lasts longer.
items.misconception: The resting potential cannot be maintained, so the axon can no longer produce any action potentials at all.
items.why: Voltage-gated channels are the channels students learn about in most detail, so they are assumed to be responsible for every stage, including rest. Voltage-gated channels open only during an action potential. The resting potential is generated by pumping and by the membrane's much greater permeability to potassium ions than to sodium ions through separate leak channels.
items.specStatementText: Voltage-gated channels drive depolarization and repolarization
items.random_wrong: Repolarization is unaffected, because the sodium–potassium pump returns the membrane potential to its resting value.

items.q: How do local currents propagate an action potential along an axon?
items.correct: Sodium ions that entered diffuse along the inside of the axon to the next region, bringing it to threshold so its sodium channels open.
items.misconception: Sodium ions that entered at the start travel along the whole axon to its end, carrying the depolarization with them.
items.why: Arrows drawn along an axon to show the direction of the impulse are read as showing the path of the ions themselves. An action potential is propagated along the fibre: at each point sodium ions cross the membrane into the axon, and the ions that entered spread only to the neighbouring region. The impulse travels; the individual ions do not.
items.specStatementText: Local currents carry the action potential along
items.random_wrong: Sodium ions that entered diffuse to the next region and depolarize it fully, so no voltage-gated channels are needed there.

items.q: An axon is cooled so that diffusion of ions becomes slower. Which prediction about conduction of impulses along it is correct?
items.correct: Conduction is slower, because local currents take longer to bring each adjacent region of membrane to threshold.
items.misconception: Conduction is unchanged, because each region is depolarized directly by the one before it without any diffusion of ions.
items.why: If the local current is thought of as 'the impulse moving along', it seems to carry the whole depolarization with it, and the regeneration of the action potential at each point is missed. Diffusion of sodium ions inside and outside the axon reduces the membrane potential of the adjacent region until the threshold potential is reached. Its voltage-gated sodium channels then open and the action potential is regenerated there at full size.
items.specStatementText: Local currents carry the action potential along
items.random_wrong: Conduction is slower, because the sodium ions take longer to travel from one end of the axon to the other.

items.q: An oscilloscope trace of an axon shows a steady −70 mV, then a rapid rise to +30 mV at 1 ms, a fall back through −70 mV by 3 ms, a brief dip to −80 mV, and a return to −70 mV. What is happening between 1 ms and 3 ms?
items.correct: Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels are open and potassium ions are leaving the axon.
items.misconception: Depolarization: the membrane potential is becoming more negative as the polarity is being removed from it.
items.why: The prefix 'de-' is read as 'going down', and 'negative' is associated with going down, so a fall in potential is assumed. Students also equate 'polarized' with 'positive'. A polarized membrane has a difference in charge across it, negative inside at rest. Depolarization reduces or reverses this difference, making the inside less negative and then positive (about +30 mV).
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.random_wrong: Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels are open and potassium ions are entering the axon.

items.q: An oscilloscope trace covering 60 ms shows 15 action potentials. What is the frequency of impulses?
items.correct: 250 impulses per second
items.misconception: 0.25 impulses per second
items.why: Oscilloscope time axes are labelled in milliseconds and the unit conversion is skipped, giving a value one thousand times too small. Convert milliseconds to seconds before dividing: 60 ms is 0.060 s. Frequency in impulses per second = number of spikes ÷ time in seconds.
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.random_wrong: 4 impulses per second

items.q: Two oscilloscope traces were recorded from the same sensory neuron. With a weak stimulus there were 5 action potentials in 100 ms; with a strong stimulus there were 20 action potentials in 100 ms. In both traces every action potential peaked at +30 mV. What do the traces show?
items.correct: Stimulus strength is coded by the frequency of impulses, while the size of each action potential stays fixed.
items.misconception: The recording must be faulty, because a stronger stimulus should produce action potentials with a higher peak.
items.why: On almost every other graph a bigger effect is a taller bar or peak, so students read amplitude as intensity. The size of an action potential is fixed by the ion gradients and channels, not by the stimulus. Stimulus strength is coded by the number of impulses per second, which can be measured from the trace.
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.random_wrong: The stronger stimulus made each impulse travel faster, so more of them reached the electrode in the time available.

items.q: Which statement explains saltatory conduction in a myelinated nerve fibre?
items.correct: Ion channels and pumps are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier, so action potentials occur only at the nodes and the impulse passes from node to node.
items.misconception: Action potentials occur along the entire membrane of the fibre, but the myelin makes each of them develop more quickly.
items.why: Students carry over the picture of propagation in a non-myelinated fibre and assume myelin adds speed without changing the mechanism. Ion pumps and channels are clustered at nodes of Ranvier, and the action potential is propagated from node to node. Depolarizing only the nodes, rather than the whole membrane, is what makes saltatory conduction faster.
items.specStatementText: Myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node
items.random_wrong: The myelin sheath conducts the electrical current along the fibre, so the impulse travels through the myelin between the nodes.

items.q: Why does a myelinated fibre conduct impulses faster than a non-myelinated fibre of the same diameter?
items.correct: Depolarization has to occur only at the nodes, so far fewer regions of membrane are depolarized along the length of the fibre.
items.misconception: A myelinated fibre has fewer nodes than a non-myelinated one, and it is the nodes that slow the impulse down.
items.why: Gaps in insulation on a wire would be a fault, so the nodes are seen as imperfections rather than as the sites where the action potential occurs. The nodes are essential: they are the only places on a myelinated fibre where voltage-gated channels are clustered and where the action potential can be regenerated. Saltatory conduction from node to node achieves faster impulses.
items.specStatementText: Myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node
items.random_wrong: Myelin is a good conductor of electricity, so the current flows through it faster than it can flow through the cytoplasm of the axon.

items.q: Cocaine binds to the transporter proteins that return dopamine to the presynaptic neuron. What effect does this have at a dopamine synapse?
items.correct: Dopamine remains in the synaptic cleft and continues to bind to postsynaptic receptors, so the postsynaptic neuron is stimulated for longer.
items.misconception: Dopamine cannot bind to its postsynaptic receptors because they are blocked, so the postsynaptic neuron receives less stimulation than normal.
items.why: 'Blocks' is the word used for cocaine's action, and blocking is assumed to happen at the receptor and to reduce the signal. Cocaine blocks reuptake of the neurotransmitter: it binds to the transporter proteins that would return dopamine to the presynaptic neuron. With reuptake blocked, dopamine continues to bind to postsynaptic receptors and stimulation is prolonged.
items.specStatementText: Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
items.random_wrong: Transmission is inhibited, because any drug that acts at a synapse prevents the postsynaptic neuron from firing.

items.q: How do neonicotinoid pesticides block synaptic transmission in insects?
items.correct: They bind to acetylcholine receptors at the insect's synapses, so acetylcholine can no longer transmit signals across them.
items.misconception: They block the reuptake of acetylcholine into the presynaptic neuron, so the insect's synapses soon run out of neurotransmitter.
items.why: Two exogenous chemicals are learned together, and their mechanisms are swapped or merged into a single 'blocks the synapse' idea. Neonicotinoids are pesticides that block synaptic transmission by binding to acetylcholine receptors in the insect's nervous system. Cocaine is the example of a drug that blocks reuptake of the neurotransmitter.
items.specStatementText: Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
items.random_wrong: They inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, so acetylcholine is not broken down at all after it has been released.

items.q: What happens at the postsynaptic membrane when an inhibitory neurotransmitter binds to its receptors?
items.correct: Channels open that make the inside more negative than the resting potential, so the membrane is hyperpolarized and further from threshold.
items.misconception: Channels open that depolarize the membrane, but by a smaller amount than an excitatory neurotransmitter would.
items.why: Students assume every neurotransmitter works the same way, opening sodium channels, and that 'inhibitory' just means 'weaker'. Inhibitory neurotransmitters open channels that let negative ions in or positive ions out, so the postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarized and moves further from the threshold potential.
items.specStatementText: Inhibitory neurotransmitters make the inside more negative
items.random_wrong: Channels open that make the inside more positive than the resting potential, which is called hyperpolarization.

items.q: A postsynaptic neuron has a resting potential of −70 mV and a threshold of −55 mV. At the same moment it receives two excitatory inputs, each producing a +8 mV change, and one inhibitory input producing a −6 mV change. What is the result?
items.correct: No action potential, because the combined change takes the membrane only to −60 mV.
items.misconception: An action potential, because the two excitatory inputs alone take the membrane to −54 mV.
items.why: Students treat excitation and inhibition as two independent switches rather than as opposite changes to the same membrane potential. Summation combines the effects of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters on the one postsynaptic membrane. The net change in membrane potential decides whether threshold is reached.
items.specStatementText: Inputs add up, and the outcome is all or nothing
items.random_wrong: Two action potentials, one triggered by each of the two excitatory inputs that arrive.

items.q: Which statement about summation at a postsynaptic neuron is correct?
items.correct: Postsynaptic potentials from several presynaptic neurons add together, and an action potential results only if threshold is reached.
items.misconception: Each impulse arriving from any presynaptic neuron produces its own action potential in the postsynaptic neuron.
items.why: Synapses are usually drawn as a one-to-one relay between two neurons, which suggests every incoming impulse is simply passed on. Multiple presynaptic neurons interact at a postsynaptic neuron. Their excitatory and inhibitory effects are summed, and an action potential is produced only if the combined depolarization reaches threshold.
items.specStatementText: Inputs add up, and the outcome is all or nothing
items.random_wrong: Postsynaptic potentials are all-or-nothing, so each one is either a full-sized action potential or nothing at all.

items.q: Eating chilli peppers causes a burning pain in the mouth. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Capsaicin opens channels for positive ions in free nerve endings, so threshold is reached and impulses pass to the brain, where pain is perceived.
items.misconception: Capsaicin raises the temperature of the tissue in the mouth, and this heat is what the free nerve endings then detect.
items.why: Chilli is described as 'hot' and the sensation is identical to burning, so the cause is assumed to be heat. Free nerve endings have channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or chemicals such as capsaicin. Because capsaicin opens the same channels, the same impulses reach the brain and the same pain is perceived.
items.specStatementText: Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain
items.random_wrong: Capsaicin stimulates free nerve endings, which perceive the pain in the mouth and then send a report of it to the brain.

items.q: A local anaesthetic blocks the voltage-gated sodium channels in the sensory neurons of a patch of skin. A hot object is then placed on the skin, but no pain is felt. Why?
items.correct: Positive ions still enter the free nerve endings, but no impulses can be propagated to the brain, where pain is perceived.
items.misconception: The channels that respond to heat are voltage-gated, so they are blocked too and no positive ions can enter.
items.why: Voltage-gated channels are the only channels studied in detail for action potentials, and students generalize them to every channel in a neuron. The channels in free nerve endings open in response to a stimulus such as high temperature, acid or capsaicin. The entry of positively charged ions through them causes the threshold potential to be reached, and only then do voltage-gated channels open to produce impulses.
items.specStatementText: Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain
items.random_wrong: The skin is where pain is perceived, and the anaesthetic has stopped the skin from perceiving the heat.

items.q: Why is consciousness described as an emergent property of the brain?
items.correct: It arises from the interaction of very many neurons and is not a property of any individual neuron.
items.misconception: It is stored in a particular small group of neurons in the brain that are specialized for consciousness.
items.why: Brain functions are often mapped to regions, so students expect consciousness to have a location in the same way that vision does. Consciousness is a property that emerges from the interaction of individual neurons in the brain. It is a consequence of interaction, not a property of any one neuron or small group of neurons.
items.specStatementText: Consciousness emerges from neurons interacting
items.random_wrong: Each neuron in the brain contributes a small amount of consciousness, and these amounts add up to the whole.

items.q: Is a nerve the same thing as a neuron?
items.correct: No. A neuron is a single cell of the nervous system; a nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres belonging to many neurons.
items.misconception: A nerve is a single neuron, so the words 'nerve' and 'neuron' mean the same thing.
items.why: Everyday language and early science courses talk about 'nerves carrying messages', and the similar words are met before the cell-level structure of the nervous system is taught. Neurons are cells within the nervous system. Each has a cell body of cytoplasm and a nucleus with nerve fibres projecting from it. A nerve is a bundle of many such fibres from many neurons, held together by connective tissue.
items.specStatementText: A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are nerve fibres part of the neuron?
items.correct: Yes. Axons and dendrites are elongated projections of the neuron's own cytoplasm and membrane.
items.misconception: Nerve fibres are separate wire-like structures that connect neurons together, rather than parts of the neuron itself.
items.why: Simplified diagrams draw the cell body as the 'cell' and the fibres as lines joining it to other cells, and the wiring analogy for the nervous system suggests cells connected by external wires. Cytoplasm and a nucleus form the cell body of a neuron, with elongated nerve fibres of varying length projecting from it. The fibres are part of the cell, enclosed by its plasma membrane, and impulses are conducted along them.
items.specStatementText: A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the sodium–potassium pump need ATP?
items.correct: Yes. It moves both ions against their concentration gradients by active transport, using energy from ATP.
items.misconception: The sodium–potassium pump is a channel through which the ions diffuse, so it works without ATP.
items.why: Pumps and channels are both membrane proteins that let ions cross, and the difference between facilitated diffusion and active transport is often blurred by the time neurons are studied. Energy from ATP drives the pumping of sodium and potassium ions in opposite directions across the plasma membrane. The pump moves ions against their concentration gradients, which diffusion through a channel can never do.
items.specStatementText: Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are nerve impulses chemical signals carried along the axon?
items.correct: No. Along the axon the impulse is electrical, a change in membrane potential caused by ion movement; chemical neurotransmitters are used only at synapses.
items.misconception: A nerve impulse consists of neurotransmitter molecules travelling along the nerve fibre.
items.why: Students learn that the nervous system uses 'chemical messengers' and generalize the synaptic mechanism to the whole neuron. A nerve impulse is an action potential propagated along a nerve fibre, and it is electrical because it involves movement of positively charged ions. Neurotransmitters carry the signal only across the synaptic cleft between cells.
items.specStatementText: A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do larger animals have faster nerve impulses?
items.correct: No. Across animals, conduction speed is negatively correlated with animal size; it is positively correlated with axon diameter and much increased by myelination.
items.misconception: Bigger animals have faster nerve impulses, because they are bigger and their nerves must be bigger too.
items.why: Students assume that everything scales with body size and that a large animal must have larger axons; they also confuse the length of a nerve with its diameter. Conduction speed of nerve impulses is negatively correlated with animal size but positively correlated with axon diameter. Very fast conduction in large mammals depends on myelination rather than on wide axons.
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does axon diameter affect the speed of a nerve impulse?
items.correct: Yes. Conduction speed is positively correlated with axon diameter, which is why the squid giant axon conducts far faster than narrow non-myelinated fibres.
items.misconception: Only myelination affects conduction speed; the diameter of the axon makes no difference.
items.why: Myelination is the difference most textbooks emphasize, and diameter is easily overlooked because both fibres in a myelinated-versus-non-myelinated comparison are usually drawn the same width. Two factors are compared in the syllabus: giant axons of squid conduct faster than smaller non-myelinated fibres because of their diameter, and myelinated fibres conduct faster than non-myelinated fibres because of saltatory conduction.
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a strong correlation prove that one variable causes the other?
items.correct: No. A correlation shows an association; it cannot by itself establish cause, which requires a controlled experiment or a known mechanism.
items.misconception: If the correlation coefficient is close to 1 or −1, the independent variable must be causing the change in the dependent variable.
items.why: Correlations are usually presented with the axes labelled 'independent' and 'dependent', which suggests cause and effect, and strong correlations are described as 'explaining' variation. Correlation coefficients measure the strength of an association, and R² measures how much variation is explained statistically, but neither shows causation. A correlation may arise from a third variable or by chance.
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does R² = 0.81 mean that 81% of the data points follow the trend?
items.correct: No. R² is the proportion of the variation in the dependent variable that is explained by the independent variable, not a count of points.
items.misconception: R² (or r) is the fraction of the data points that fit the correlation.
items.why: Percentages are usually met as 'x out of every hundred', so a value like 81% is read as 81 of every 100 fibres, samples or points. The coefficient of determination evaluates the degree to which variation in the independent variable explains the variation in the dependent variable. It refers to the spread of the values, not to how many points lie on the line.
items.specStatementText: Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are synapses found only between two neurons?
items.correct: No. Synapses are junctions between neurons and also between neurons and effector cells such as muscle fibres and gland cells.
items.misconception: A synapse is always a junction between two neurons; neurons stimulate muscles directly without a synapse.
items.why: Almost every synapse diagram shows two neurons, and the neuromuscular junction is often given a separate name so students do not classify it as a synapse. Synapses are junctions between neurons and between neurons and effector cells. A neuromuscular junction is a synapse at which a motor neuron releases acetylcholine onto a muscle fibre.
items.specStatementText: Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does neurotransmitter cross the synaptic cleft?
items.correct: By diffusion through the fluid in the cleft, down its concentration gradient.
items.misconception: Neurotransmitter is actively transported across the cleft by carrier proteins.
items.why: Students learn that 'the synapse needs ATP' and that transmission is fast, and they assume anything fast or energy-requiring must be active transport. Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. The cleft is only about 20 nm wide, so diffusion is very fast. ATP is used for pumping ions and for reuptake, not for crossing the cleft.
items.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a trace shows 15 spikes, is the frequency 15 impulses per second?
items.correct: Only if the trace covers exactly one second. The frequency is the number of spikes divided by the time the trace covers, in seconds.
items.misconception: The number of spikes visible on the trace is the number of impulses per second, whatever time the trace covers.
items.why: Students count the spikes and stop, treating the count as the answer, because the time axis is easily ignored when it is not marked in seconds. The number of impulses per second is measured by counting the action potentials and dividing by the time covered by the trace in seconds. Fifteen spikes in 60 ms is 15 ÷ 0.060 = 250 impulses per second.
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is frequency found by dividing the time by the number of spikes?
items.correct: No. Frequency is the number of spikes divided by the time; dividing time by number gives the interval between spikes instead.
items.misconception: Impulses per second is worked out as time divided by the number of spikes.
items.why: Students know one quantity is divided by the other but not which way round, and the calculation of the interval between spikes is confused with the calculation of frequency. Frequency = number of impulses ÷ time in seconds. Fifteen spikes in 60 ms gives 15 ÷ 0.060 = 250 impulses per second; 60 ÷ 15 = 4 ms is the time between spikes, not the frequency.
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a stronger stimulus make the impulse travel faster along the axon?
items.correct: No. Conduction speed depends on the fibre (its diameter and whether it is myelinated), not on the stimulus; a stronger stimulus produces impulses more often.
items.misconception: A stronger stimulus produces impulses that travel faster along the nerve fibre.
items.why: Students know that a strong stimulus produces a faster response overall and attribute this to faster conduction rather than to a higher frequency of impulses. The speed of a nerve impulse is a property of the fibre. What changes with stimulus strength is the number of impulses per second, which can be measured from an oscilloscope trace.
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the resting potential shown as 0 mV on an oscilloscope trace?
items.correct: No. The resting potential is a steady line at about −70 mV; 0 mV is crossed only briefly during the action potential.
items.misconception: The flat baseline between spikes on the trace is at 0 mV, because the neuron is 'off' at rest.
items.why: A flat baseline on most graphs represents zero, and 'resting' suggests no potential at all. A resting neuron is polarized, with the inside about 70 mV negative relative to the outside. The trace therefore rests at about −70 mV and the spike passes through 0 mV on the way up to about +30 mV.
items.specStatementText: Reading an oscilloscope trace
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every drug that acts at a synapse reduce transmission?
items.correct: No. Some, like cocaine, increase stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron by keeping neurotransmitter in the cleft; others, like neonicotinoids, block transmission.
items.misconception: Any drug or chemical acting at a synapse inhibits it and stops the postsynaptic neuron firing.
items.why: Drugs and poisons are assumed to 'shut things down', and inhibitory effects are the ones most often described. Exogenous chemicals can either block synaptic transmission (neonicotinoids at acetylcholine receptors) or enhance it (cocaine, by blocking dopamine reuptake so that stimulation continues).
items.specStatementText: Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do neonicotinoids work by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase?
items.correct: No. Neonicotinoids bind to the acetylcholine receptors themselves; inhibiting acetylcholinesterase is the mechanism of other pesticides such as organophosphates.
items.misconception: Neonicotinoids kill insects by inhibiting the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, so acetylcholine accumulates.
items.why: Students who have met enzyme inhibitors expect any pesticide acting at an acetylcholine synapse to target the enzyme, and the two classes of insecticide are confused. Neonicotinoids block synaptic transmission by binding to acetylcholine receptors at synapses in the insect's nervous system, so that acetylcholine can no longer pass the signal across them.
items.specStatementText: Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does hyperpolarization make the inside of the membrane more positive?
items.correct: No. Hyperpolarization makes the inside more negative than the resting potential, for example −75 mV instead of −70 mV.
items.misconception: 'Hyper' means more, so a hyperpolarized membrane is more positive than usual.
items.why: The prefix 'hyper-' is met in words like 'hyperactive', so it is read as 'more' in the sense of higher, which is then equated with more positive. Polarized means having a charge difference across the membrane, negative inside. Hyperpolarized means even more polarized: the inside is more negative than at rest, so it is further from threshold.
items.specStatementText: Inhibitory neurotransmitters make the inside more negative
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do inhibitory neurotransmitters act by stopping the presynaptic neuron releasing neurotransmitter?
items.correct: No. They are themselves released by a presynaptic neuron and act on the postsynaptic membrane, hyperpolarizing it.
items.misconception: An inhibitory neurotransmitter prevents release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic neuron, so nothing reaches the postsynaptic cell.
items.why: Inhibition is pictured as 'switching off the source', and the idea that inhibition can be an active effect on the postsynaptic membrane is unfamiliar. Inhibitory neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane and open channels that make the inside more negative. The postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarized, generating an inhibitory postsynaptic potential.
items.specStatementText: Inhibitory neurotransmitters make the inside more negative
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are postsynaptic potentials all-or-nothing?
items.correct: No. Postsynaptic potentials are graded and can add together; it is the action potential they may trigger that is all-or-nothing.
items.misconception: An excitatory postsynaptic potential is the same thing as an action potential, so it is either full-sized or absent.
items.why: Both are 'potentials' and both involve depolarization, and the all-or-nothing rule is applied to every electrical event in a neuron. Excitatory postsynaptic potentials vary in size with the amount of neurotransmitter and can be summed. The consequence of summation is all-or-nothing: either threshold is reached and a full action potential follows, or it is not and no action potential occurs.
items.specStatementText: Inputs add up, and the outcome is all or nothing
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where is pain perceived?
items.correct: In the brain. The free nerve endings in the skin detect the stimulus, but the sensation of pain arises when the impulses reach the brain.
items.misconception: Pain is perceived in the skin at the site of the injury, and the nerves then report it to the brain.
items.why: Pain is felt as being located in the injured part of the body, so the perception is assumed to happen there. Entry of positively charged ions causes the threshold potential to be reached in the free nerve ending, and nerve impulses then pass through the neurons to the brain, where pain is perceived. The nerve endings detect; the brain perceives.
items.specStatementText: Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are pain receptors separate cells that pass a signal to a sensory neuron?
items.correct: No. The receptors for pain are the free nerve endings of the sensory neurons themselves; the ion channels are in the neuron's own membrane.
items.misconception: Pain is detected by specialized receptor cells in the skin that release neurotransmitter onto a sensory neuron.
items.why: Other senses studied earlier, such as taste and hearing, do use separate receptor cells, so the same arrangement is expected for pain. Pain is perceived by neurons with free nerve endings in the skin. The nerve endings have channels for positively charged ions, and their opening depolarizes the neuron directly to threshold.
items.specStatementText: Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an emergent property just the sum of the properties of the parts?
items.correct: No. An emergent property arises from the interactions between the components and is not present in any of them, even in a small amount.
items.misconception: Each neuron contributes a small amount of consciousness, and these amounts add up to the consciousness of the whole brain.
items.why: Adding up is the familiar way a whole relates to its parts, and 'emergent' is not distinguished from 'total'. Emergent properties are consequences of interaction. No single neuron is conscious to any degree; consciousness appears only when very many neurons interact.
items.specStatementText: Consciousness emerges from neurons interacting
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is consciousness produced by a particular neurotransmitter?
items.correct: No. Consciousness emerges from the interaction of neurons across the brain; no single chemical produces it.
items.misconception: Consciousness is caused by a specific neurotransmitter released in the brain when a person is awake.
items.why: Popular accounts link single chemicals to single mental states (dopamine to pleasure, for example), so a chemical for consciousness is expected. Consciousness is a property that emerges from the interaction of individual neurons in the brain. It cannot be reduced to one molecule or one signal.
items.specStatementText: Consciousness emerges from neurons interacting
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
